Background and aims Inflammation plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). This involves neutrophil activation and the local release of pro-inflammatory mediators. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in coronary thrombosis has been linked to poor short-term prognosis following STEMI, but the usefulness of specific circulating NET components as prognostic markers is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the NET-specific marker nucleosomal citrullinated histone H3 (H3Cit-DNA) and other classical inflammatory markers to predict adverse events after STEMI. Methods This is a single-center retrospective cohort study of patients with STEMI undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) from 2015 to 2019. We analyzed the association between serum H3Cit-DNA levels, double-stranded DNA, and classical inflammatory markers –such us interleukin (IL) 6 and 1β, TNF-α, and C-reactive protein (CRP)– on admission and the occurrence of major cardiovascular events (MACE), including death, reinfarction, urgent revascularization, or heart failure, after STEMI. Results A total of 487 patients were studied, of which 380 were men [78%]; mean [SD] age of patients was 63 [13] years, and median [95%CI] follow-up was 5.4 [5.2-5.5] years. Median [IQR] H3Cit level was 179.30 [105.30-281.47] ng/ml. No relevant association was found between H3Cit-DNA levels and 30-day mortality (OR, 1.03 [95%CI, 0.71-1.50], p = 0.861) or MACE (0.98 [0.72-1.32], p = 0.879), Killip class (0.95 [0.74-1.21], p = 0.664), or left ventricular ejection fraction (ref.cat. > 50%; < 35%, RRR 1.01 [95%CI, 0.74-1.38], p = 0.952; 35-50%, 1.26 [1.07-1.48], p = 0.005]. Adding CRP and IL-6 levels as covariates to a model based on classical risk factors significantly improved the prediction of MACE at 30 days after STEMI (IDI 0.13; NRI 0.32, p < 0.05). Conclusions Circulating levels of the NET marker H3Cit-DNA at the time of primary PCI were not predictive of cardiovascular events following STEMI. In contrast, the classical inflammatory markers CRP and interleukin-6 significantly enhanced the discriminative capacity of a clinical 30-day risk prediction model. The contact person (Belén Ruiz-Antorán) will be responsible for providing the data if necessary. Introduction Inflammation plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis. In ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), the initial inflammatory response is typically triggered by plaque rupture and coronary occlusion at the culprit lesion site. This process encompasses the activation of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMN), the recruitment of monocytes, and the local release of pro-inflammatory mediators, such as interleukins (IL) [ 1 ]. The acute cytokine surge enhances neutrophil activation, promotes the release of granule enzymes such as myeloperoxidase (MPO) and catalase, and triggers an oxidative response [ 2 ]. During this phase of post-STEMI inflammation, processes that worsen the detrimental effects of inflammation –particularly involving key cytokines (e.g., IL-1 and IL-6) and PMN-induced neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation– are especially active, further amplifying their harmful impact [ 3 ]. Local inflammation evolves into a systemic response characterized by elevated inflammatory biomarkers, making early pro-inflammatory markers valuable tools for risk stratification after STEMI. Among the biomarkers of inflammation in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, C-reactive protein (CRP) is the most extensively studied. CRP, an acute-phase protein, is predominantly produced by hepatocytes under the influence of cytokines such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α [ 4 ]. Elevated CRP levels are associated with an increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events. Some but not all studies have found that serum СRР predicts the risk of a recurrent in-hospital cardiac event [ 5 ] or 30-day or long-term mortality after STEMI [ 6 , 7 ]. Interleukin-1β amplifies inflammation by promoting its own expression in various cell types and stimulating the production of IL-6 [ 8 ]. Blocking IL-1β and IL-6 receptors with specific antibodies has been shown to reduce circulating CRP levels [ 9 , 10 ]. Elevated IL-6 levels are associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) following myocardial infarction [ 11 ]. On the other hand, emerging experimental and clinical evidence indicates that the formation of NETs in coronary thrombosis exerts harmful effects. NETs are modified chromatin structures released by neutrophils in response to specific stimuli, bound to cytoplasmic and granular proteins. Although NETs play a protective role against pathogens, dysregulated NETs exhibit strong proinflammatory and prothrombotic properties. In patients with STEMI, the presence of NETs in coronary thrombi is associated with larger infarcts and worse short-term outcomes [ 12 – 14 ]. The NET-specific circulating marker, citrullinated histone H3 DNA complex (H3Cit-DNA), plays a central role in NET formation. A standardized detection method is now available [ 15 ], although its clinical applicability in this context remains uncertain. The primary objective of this study was to assess the utility of peripheral H3Cit-DNA levels and classical inflammatory markers in predicting adverse outcomes after STEMI.

extracted_data.document_summary: A single-center retrospective cohort study evaluated the prognostic utility of the NET-specific marker H3Cit-DNA and classical inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, dsDNA) for predicting adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) within 30 days after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) in patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). The study found that circulating H3Cit-DNA levels were not predictive of cardiovascular events, but CRP and IL-6 significantly improved the discriminative capacity of a 30-day risk prediction model for MACE.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Prognostic marker evaluation in patients post-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) undergoing Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single-center retrospective cohort study analyzed serum markers from 487 STEMI patients (2015-2019) on admission who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 12 hours of symptom onset. Patients received a loading dose of acetylsalicylic acid and a second antiplatelet agent (clopidogrel, ticagrelor, or prasugrel) prior to PCI, and 53% received GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide). Most patients (92%) were revascularized with stents. No dose-response comparisons for these treatments in relation to biomarker levels or specific PCI intensity parameters were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not predictive of major cardiovascular events or mortality, though a specific association with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was observed.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median [IQR] H3Cit level was 179.30 [105.30-281.47] ng/ml. No significant association was found with 30-day mortality (OR, 1.03 [95%CI, 0.71-1.50], p = 0.861), MACE (0.98 [0.72-1.32], p = 0.879), or Killip class (0.95 [0.74-1.21], p = 0.664). A significant association was found for left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 35-50% (RRR 1.26 [95%CI, 1.07-1.48], p = 0.005) compared to > 50%, but not for LVEF < 35% (RRR 1.01 [95%CI, 0.74-1.38], p = 0.952).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A NET-specific marker playing a central role in PAD4-dependent neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, where dysregulated NETs exhibit strong proinflammatory and prothrombotic properties.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prognostic evaluation at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) on admission after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates limited utility in assessing the inflammatory state or predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) or mortality after STEMI, though a mild association with reduced Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF) was observed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detectable in 80% of patients, CRP levels were significantly associated with Killip classification, LVEF, MACE, and 30-day mortality after STEMI in univariable analysis. Adding CRP and IL-6 to the clinical model significantly improved 30-day MACE prediction (IDI 0.13; NRI 0.32, p < 0.05; likelihood-ratio test p < 0.0001; AUC improved from 0.866 to 0.884).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A widely used acute-phase protein and marker of inflammation, predominantly produced by hepatocytes under the influence of cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-α.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prognostic evaluation at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) on admission after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), integrated into a 30-day MACE prediction model.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels indicate an increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events and have significant prognostic value for MACE and other clinical endpoints after STEMI, improving the discriminative ability of a 30-day STEMI clinical risk prediction model for risk stratification and guiding inflammation-targeted therapies.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detectable in 41% of patients, IL-6 levels were significantly associated with Killip classification, LVEF, MACE, and 30-day mortality after STEMI in univariable analysis. Adding CRP and IL-6 to the clinical model significantly improved 30-day MACE prediction (IDI 0.13; NRI 0.32, p < 0.05; likelihood-ratio test p < 0.0001; AUC improved from 0.866 to 0.884).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A pro-inflammatory cytokine and inflammatory marker that amplifies inflammation, stimulates the production of itself and other inflammatory markers like CRP, with clinical evidence supporting its prognostic value in acute coronary syndrome.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prognostic evaluation at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) on admission after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), integrated into a 30-day MACE prediction model.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels are associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) following myocardial infarction and have significant prognostic value for MACE and other clinical endpoints after STEMI, improving the discriminative ability of a 30-day STEMI clinical risk prediction model for risk stratification and guiding inflammation-targeted therapies.
